common_name: Downing Mulberry (Historic American Sweet Black-Fruited Mulberry)

planting.note: Plant a rooted cutting or container tree in late winter to early spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Downing is one of the oldest named American mulberry selections and needs no pollinator to fruit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Downing was selected in the mid-1800s from the mulberry plantings established during the era of American silk-culture experiments and became the first widely distributed named mulberry cultivar in the United States, prized above seedling trees for its consistently excellent flavor. The tree bears an abundance of long, cylindrical, glossy black fruit over a several-week summer harvest window, with a rich, sweet, low-acid flavor good for fresh eating, preserves, and drying. It is self-fertile, vigorous, and adaptable to a wide range of soils, tolerating heat and some drought once established, though it lacks the extreme cold hardiness of the later alba-rubra hybrid selections bred for northern climates. Site away from patios, walkways, and parked cars, since the juicy ripe fruit drops steadily and stains hard surfaces.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Maine Organic Farmers and Gardeners Association

planting.note: Plant a container or balled-and-burlapped tree in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; as an all-male clone it must be propagated by cuttings rather than seed and never sets fruit.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, siting away from walks and drives since the wide-spreading surface roots can heave paving as the tree matures. Fruitless is a male clone of white mulberry selected specifically because it produces no berries, giving gardeners the dense, fast-growing shade canopy and glossy foliage of mulberry without the mess of dropped, staining fruit that plagues fruiting seedling trees. It grows rapidly into a broad, rounded shade tree that tolerates heat, drought, poor soil, and urban pollution once established, making it a popular low-maintenance choice for patios, driveways, and parking areas where fruiting trees would be a nuisance. Prune while young to establish strong scaffold branching, since mature wood can be brittle in storms.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Zenjimaru is a pollination-variant type, so planting near another kaki cultivar improves seed set and sweetness.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Zenjimaru is among the oldest named persimmon cultivars in cultivation, traced to a temple orchard in Japan roughly 800 years ago, and is historically important as the earliest documented source of the naturally sweet, non-astringent trait later bred into many modern kaki cultivars. It is a pollination-variant type: fruit that develops seeds from cross-pollination loses its astringency and becomes sweet and edible while still firm, while unpollinated, seedless fruit stays astringent until it softens fully. The tree bears small to medium, round, orange-red fruit with a thin glossy skin and rich, sugary flavor, and is notably vigorous, disease-resistant, and productive across a range of soils and climates. Thin heavy fruit set in early summer to reduce limb strain, and harvest in mid to late fall once fruit colors fully.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant on a sturdy trellis or arbor in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun, siting a compatible male Actinidia arguta vine nearby since Jumbo is a female cultivar and will not set fruit alone.

directions: Jumbo is a female hardy kiwi selection bred for noticeably larger, smooth-skinned berries than most arguta cultivars, with individual fruit approaching an ounce and a sweet, citrus-tinged flavor eaten whole, skin and all, with no peeling needed. Vines are vigorous twining climbers that require a permanent, heavily built trellis or arbor and benefit from annual winter pruning to control size and renew fruiting wood. Plants begin bearing in their third or fourth year and are exceptionally cold-hardy, tolerating winter temperatures well below zero once established. Harvest in early to mid fall by taste-testing a few berries, since the green skin shows little visible color change at ripeness.
